sense: what something is for, the aim

terms.gloss: for the purpose of, for the sake of
terms.grammar: ablative of causa, placed after a genitive: a noun, a gerund or a gerundive
evidence: Plin. Ep. 9.36.3: nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: in the best prose “almost always referring to the future, and implying a purpose”. For “on purpose” see mean (intend): cōnsultō.

terms.grammar: conjunction, with the subjunctive; nē for a purpose to be avoided
evidence: Cic. Off. 3.42: ēnītī et contendere dēbet quam maximē possit, ut vincat
Caes. BG 1.48: eō cōnsiliō utī frūmentō commeātūque … Caesarem interclūderet
terms.comment: The commonest way to state a purpose: Latin uses a clause where English uses the noun (vēnī ut tē vidērem, the purpose of my visit was to see you). After verbs of going, the supine in -um: lūsum it, he goes off to play (Hor. S. 1.5.48).

terms.gloss: a purpose, an intention: what someone means to do
evidence: Caes. BG 1.48: eō cōnsiliō utī frūmentō commeātūque … Caesarem interclūderet
Ter. Eun. 1024: quā spē aut quō cōnsiliō hūc īmus?
terms.comment: Eō cōnsiliō ut, with the purpose of; quō cōnsiliō?, for what purpose? Also a decision and advice (see decision).

terms.gloss: the end a thing serves, its purpose
evidence: Cic. Off. 1.138: domum … cujus fīnis est ūsus
Quint. 2.17.22: omnēs artēs habēre fīnem aliquem prōpositum, ad quem tendunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of the purpose a thing exists for; a person’s own aim is rather cōnsilium or prōpositum (Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Leg. 1.4: quōrsum tandem aut cūr ista quaeris?
terms.comment: Lewis & Short: “to what purpose? to what end? with what view? for what?”; quōrsus, inquam, istuc?, what are you getting at? (Cic. Brut. 292, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: is cum in pāce īnstituisset puerōs ante urbem lūsūs exercendīque causā prōdūcere
phrases.english: he had made it his practice in peacetime to take the boys out in front of the city for play and exercise

phrases.latin: ōrātiōnem Graecam Latīnamve clārē et intentē nōn tam vōcis causā quam stomachī legō
phrases.english: I read a speech in Greek or Latin aloud and with energy, not so much for the sake of my voice as of my digestion

phrases.latin: lūsum it Maecēnās, dormītum ego Vergiliusque
phrases.english: Maecenas goes off to play ball, Virgil and I to sleep
‘Where can I get a stone?’ ‘What do you need it for?’ ‘Where can I get arrows?’
